Historically, Russell 2000 forward price-to-earnings multiples compress when 10-year yields surpass 6%, strategist Jill Carey Hall wrote in a note to clients. But earnings-per-share revisions were above average when yields ranged between 6% and 8%, indicating that past valuation contractions occurred in tandem with stronger earnings growth.

As a result, average small-cap returns in the 6%–7% yield range were not historically weaker. Today, Russell 2000 P/E multiples have already fallen below their historical averages seen during prior 5%–6% and 6%–7% rate regimes.

Despite these compressed valuations, structural shifts have made small caps more vulnerable to high rates than in past cycles. The negative correlation between small-cap P/E ratios and 10-year yields has hit record intensity, driven by elevated corporate leverage and a record percentage of non-earning companies in the Russell 2000. Higher rates—fueled in part by Federal Reserve rate hike expectations—pose an immediate challenge, as half of small-cap debt is short-term or floating-rate, and a growing share of long-term debt matures within the next five years, BofA noted.

BofA projects a 10-year yield of 5.0% by year-end, offering a window for small-cap recovery if yields stabilize. However, they warned that yields could stay elevated or rise further until economic data soften or financial conditions tighten. Consequently, the firm continues to recommend mid-cap stocks over small caps, pointing to mid-caps' lower rate risk and similar projected second-half earnings recovery.
